title: The Hymn to Aphrodite and Wharton's translation
short: Sappho's only poem that survives complete, given here in Henry Thornton Wharton's 1885 literal prose version; it is fr. 1 in his and in modern editions.
body: This seven-stanza prayer survives whole because the critic Dionysius of Halicarnassus, writing at Rome around 25 BC, quoted it in full as his model of the smooth, finished style; a papyrus later confirmed parts of it. The archive's text is Henry Thornton Wharton's literal prose translation from his Sappho of 1885, a book that did much to bring Sappho to late-Victorian readers. Wharton printed the Greek beside his version, together with verse renderings by earlier poets (Ambrose Philips, Swinburne and others). His prose gives the sense clause by clause but not the metre: the Greek is in Sapphic stanzas (see the note on the form). Every English word here is a translator's choice from a Greek text with a few disputed readings, two of which are glossed below.

title: broidered throne
short: Wharton reads poikilothron', 'of the many-coloured throne'; part of the tradition has poikilophron, 'of the many-coloured (subtle) mind'.
body: The poem opens with a compound epithet whose text is uncertain. Wharton's Greek reads poikilothron', 'with intricately worked (many-coloured) throne', hence his 'broidered throne' (broider is an old form of embroider). Part of the manuscript tradition has poikilophron, 'of the shifting, intricate mind', which would chime with 'weaver of wiles' that follows; Swinburne, whose versions Wharton quotes, used both ('O thou of divers-coloured mind', 'Thou of the divers-coloured seat'). Some scholars connect the -thron- element instead with throna, the flower-patterns Andromache weaves into her cloth at Iliad 22.441, so that the goddess would be 'of the many-flowered robe'. Most editors (Page, Campbell) print poikilothron', but each alternative gives a different first picture of the goddess: splendid, crafty or flowered.

title: weaver of wiles
short: Wharton's rendering of doloploke, 'wile-weaving', an epithet that admits from the start that Aphrodite works by trickery.
body: Doloploke combines dolos, 'trick, snare', with plekein, 'to plait or weave'. It belongs to a family of Greek ideas in which cunning is a kind of weaving (Odysseus and Penelope are the great epic examples), and in love poetry Aphrodite's power is regularly described as deceit. Sappho praises the goddess, as hymns must, while hinting at the danger of asking for her help: the same craft that may win the beloved is what has caused the speaker's distress. Wharton keeps an alliteration ('weaver of wiles'), and his 'daughter of Zeus' preserves the hymn habit of naming a god's parentage so that the right deity is addressed.

title: Prayer form and the Sapphic stanza
short: The poem follows the shape of a cult hymn (invocation, reminder of past help, request), in the four-line Sapphic stanza that Wharton's prose does not reproduce.
body: Greek prayers commonly have three parts: the god is named with titles; the worshipper recalls earlier favours ('if ever before thou didst hear') to oblige the god to help again; then comes the request. Sappho fills the middle part with a long narrative of a past epiphany, so that the hymn becomes a story about prayer. The 'if ever before' pattern is old: Chryses uses it to Apollo at Iliad 1.37-42 and Diomedes to Athena at Iliad 5.115-120. The metre is the Sapphic stanza, three eleven-syllable lines and a short closing line (the 'adonic'). Wharton prints the Greek in stanzas but translates into continuous prose, so his sentences run across the stanza breaks. Compare Arthur Way's verse version in this archive ('To the Queen of Love'), which imitates the stanza.

title: thy father's golden house
short: Aphrodite leaves the house of Zeus on Olympus; Greek gods' dwellings and possessions are conventionally golden.
body: In the Greek, 'golden' (chrysion) stands at the end of a stanza and could go either with the house or, running on into the next stanza, with the chariot that is yoked; editors differ, and Wharton chooses the house. Either way the gold marks the divine world as radiant and imperishable, in contrast with the 'dark earth' the goddess crosses. The journey from Olympus to Lesbos dramatises the distance between god and mortal that prayer has to bridge, and the verbs of leaving, yoking and driving give the epiphany the formality of a Homeric divine descent.

title: sparrows
short: Aphrodite's chariot is drawn by sparrows (strouthoi), birds linked with her because they were thought amorous and prolific.
body: Homeric gods drive horses; Sappho gives her goddess a team of small birds whirring their wings, an image at once charming and faintly comic. Ancient writers on natural history record that sparrows were thought lustful, which explains their association with Aphrodite (Athenaeus collects such lore). Wharton's 'flapping fast their wings' renders pukna dinnentes, 'whirling their wings thick and fast'. Several of the English versions Wharton reprints keep the sparrows (Philips: 'The car thy wanton sparrows drew'). Some critics have wondered whether Catullus's poems on Lesbia's sparrow (Carmina 2 and 3) glance at Sappho; that link is debated.

title: the dark earth
short: A Homeric formula (gaia melaina) for the earth seen from above; Sappho uses the same phrase in fr. 16 for 'the black earth'.
body: 'Dark' (melainas) is a fixed epithet of earth in epic (for example Iliad 2.699), and Sappho uses it with Homeric dignity as the goddess flies 'from heaven through mid sky'. The phrase recurs at the opening of fr. 16 ('the most beautiful thing on the black earth'), where it means 'the whole world below'. In both poems the epic diction helps Sappho set personal love in a large, almost cosmic frame.

title: smiling
short: The smile recalls Aphrodite's Homeric title 'laughter-loving' (philommeides); here it reads as amused indulgence of a familiar suppliant.
body: Aphrodite is 'laughter-loving' in Homer and Hesiod, and Sappho's participle meidiaisaisa recalls the title. In context the smile carries tone: the goddess has heard this kind of complaint before (see the repeated 'now' that follows) and treats it with affectionate irony. Critics differ on how far the humour goes: some stress the tenderness of the scene, others the gap between the speaker's agony and the goddess's calm. Either way the smile is 'immortal', a reminder that gods do not suffer love as mortals do.

title: What now ... Why now
short: Wharton's 'now' renders Greek deute, 'now again, once more', repeated three times: the goddess teases Sappho about yet another love-crisis.
body: Deute (de aute) means 'this time again'. The goddess asks what Sappho is suffering this time, why she calls this time, and whom she must persuade this time. The repetition makes the epiphany a gently comic scene of a recurring pattern, and also generalises the poem: love is not a single event but a cycle of desire, pain and prayer. Wharton's plain 'now' loses the sense of repetition. His capitals (What, Why) mark reported questions, which turn into direct speech in the next stanza, a shift Sappho makes in the Greek too.

title: mad heart
short: Greek mainolai thumoi, 'in my raving spirit': love as a kind of madness (mania), a theme later developed by Plato.
body: The thumos is the seat of feeling and impulse; the adjective mainolas, 'raving', links erotic desire with madness. Sappho returns to this territory in fr. 31, where love produces symptoms close to death. Plato's Phaedrus later counts erotic madness among the divine manias. Here the phrase is reported in the goddess's questions, which lets the speaker see her own state from outside.

anchor: What Beauty now wouldst thou draw
title: What Beauty now wouldst thou draw to love thee?
greek: τίνα δηὖτε πείθω ... ἄγην ἐς σὰν φιλότατα
short: The Greek is corrupt: Wharton's 'Beauty' loosely renders his text's Peitho, where modern editors read 'Whom must I persuade, this time, to bring back to your love?'
body: Wharton's Greek reads tina deute Peitho / mais agen es san philotata, in which Peitho ('Persuasion', a goddess of Aphrodite's train) seems to be named; his 'What Beauty ... wouldst thou draw' is a loose attempt to make sense of it. The manuscripts are damaged at this point. Modern editions (Lobel-Page, Voigt, Campbell) print a reading in which the goddess asks whom she must 'persuade' (peitho as a verb, 'I persuade') to bring back to Sappho's love. The difference matters: in the modern text Aphrodite acts as an agent of persuasion, which prepares the promises of the next stanza. Students quoting the archive's line should note that it is the 1885 reading.

title: Who wrongs thee, Sappho?
short: The poet names herself, and the goddess frames the love-trouble as an injustice (adikeei) to be put right.
body: Self-naming is rare in Sappho and gives the poem the feel of a real conversation between poet and goddess; Swinburne's 'Anactoria', which Wharton quotes, builds on this line. The verb adikein, 'to do wrong', is moral and legal language. Anne Carson argued that the next stanza describes a kind of erotic justice: the beloved who now flees, refuses gifts and does not love will be made to pursue, give and love, so that the roles are reversed. Others read the promise more simply as the standard reassurance a god gives a suppliant. The question also makes clear that the speaker's pain is caused by another person rather than by the goddess.

title: however loth
short: Wharton's 'however loth' renders kouk etheloisa, 'even unwilling'; the feminine participle is the only word in the poem that tells us the beloved is a woman.
body: The goddess promises that the beloved will love 'even against her will'. The Greek participle etheloisa is feminine; it is the single grammatical marker of the beloved's sex in the poem, and Wharton's 'she' throughout depends on it. Some earlier translators blurred or altered it. The phrase has also troubled readers morally, since it seems to promise love by compulsion; others take it as a statement of how love works (it overrides the will) rather than a wish to coerce. Wharton's archaic 'loth' (unwilling) keeps the sense without settling the question.

title: ally
short: The last word of the poem is symmachos, 'fellow-fighter in battle': the love-prayer ends in the language of war.
body: Symmachos is a military term, 'one who fights alongside'. By ending on it Sappho turns love into a campaign in which the goddess is asked to take her side. Scholars have connected the poem with Diomedes' prayer to Athena in Iliad 5, where the goddess comes to stand beside the hero; J. J. Winkler read Sappho's hymn as a deliberate reworking of that heroic scene from a woman's point of view. The ring-composition is also notable: the final stanza repeats the opening request ('come', 'release me', 'accomplish'), so the poem closes on the prayer it began with, still unanswered.
